topic: Change of Basis: Seeing the World Through Different Eyes
target_audience: University students or advanced high school students studying Linear Algebra

sections.title: The Hook: The Map Dilemma
lecture_lines: Imagine one treasure chest, but two different maps.
Alice uses a standard North-East grid.
Bob's map is tilted along a canyon.
animations: Show Alice's white (#FFFFFF) standard grid over a desert background; place a treasure chest at (3, 4).
Overlay Bob's slanted yellow (#FFFF00) grid, keeping the treasure chest at the same physical location.
Highlight the coordinate (3, 4) in Alice's grid and a different coordinate pair in Bob's grid.

sections.title: Prerequisite Refresher: What is a Basis?
lecture_lines: A basis is a set of building-block vectors.
Standard basis vectors are unit-length and perpendicular.
Every point is a unique recipe of vectors.
animations: Display the standard basis: unit vectors e1 (1,0) in red (#FF0000) and e2 (0,1) in blue (#0000FF) on a white grid (#FFFFFF).
Create vector 'v' from (0,0) to (3,2) in cyan (#00FFFF).
Trace the path to 'v' using 3 red (#FF0000) e1 steps and 2 blue (#0000FF) e2 steps.

sections.title: The New Perspective: Non-Standard Basis
lecture_lines: Bases don't have to be square.
We can define space using any independent vectors.
This creates a custom, skewed coordinate grid.
animations: Introduce basis vectors b1 (2,1) in light green (#90EE90) and b2 (-1,1) in orange (#FFA500) on the standard grid.
Fade out the standard grid and fade in a skewed light green (#90EE90) grid aligned with b1 and b2.
Show a small robot icon moving along the skewed grid to coordinates (1,1).

sections.title: The Bridge: The Change of Basis Matrix
lecture_lines: A Change of Basis matrix translates between systems.
It maps Bob's coordinates back to Alice's.
The columns are Bob's vectors in Alice's language.
This matrix morphs standard grids into Bob's.
We call this transformation matrix P.
animations: Show the Change of Basis Matrix P = [[2, -1], [1, 1]] with columns colored light green (#90EE90) and orange (#FFA500).
Animate the standard white grid (#FFFFFF) morphing into the skewed light green (#90EE90) grid.
Highlight how the columns of P correspond exactly to the coordinates of b1 and b2 in the standard grid.

sections.title: The Mathematical Transformation
lecture_lines: Multiply P by Bob's vector to find Alice's.
Use the inverse of P for the reverse.
P-inverse decodes standard vectors into custom bases.
It transforms the perspective, not the vector itself.
Math allows us to swap viewpoints instantly.
animations: Display the core formula [v]std = P * [v]B in white (#FFFFFF) at the top of the screen.
Substitute [1,1] for [v]B and multiply by matrix P to calculate the result (1,2).
Simultaneously show the vector at (1,1) in the skewed grid and its transformation to (1,2) in the standard grid.

sections.title: Real-World Application: Computer Graphics
lecture_lines: Graphics engines use this to render 3D scenes.
Characters have their own local basis.
The world has a global standard basis.
Moving cameras requires a change of basis.
This aligns the world with your view.
animations: Illustrate a 'Dragon' icon with its own local axes (forward/up) in a 'World' grid.
Rotate the Dragon and its local axes to show how its perspective changes relative to the World grid.
Project a 'Sun' object's position onto the Dragon's local axes, showing its local coordinates change during the rotation.

sections.title: Summary & Key Takeaway
lecture_lines: Vectors are absolute arrows in physical space.
Coordinates are just labels relative to a basis.
Change your basis to see the world differently.
animations: Show a static cyan (#00FFFF) arrow (vector) pointing to a fixed point in space.
Continuously rotate and scale the underlying grid lines beneath the fixed arrow.
Display changing coordinate labels (x,y) that update as the grid moves, while the arrow remains stationary.
